Consistent with a modular organisational principle, we furthermore find copy numbers of NPC/NB-associated TPR to be far higher than commonly anticipated. Together with sufficient ZC3HC1 copy numbers, our data define a model in which alternating recruitment of ZC3HC1 and TPR extends the NB's spatial and functional reach into the nuclear interior.

title: Force Induces a Collective Inactivity in Dyneins to Auto-Regulate Bidirectional Transport of Vesicles
authors: Chaudhury, D.; Kumar, A.; Sanghavi, P.; Muhuri, S.; Mitra, M. K.; Mallik, R.
abstract: The back-and-forth (bidirectional) motion of Endosomes and Phagosomes along microtubules is fundamentally important for nutrient absorption, receptor recycling, pathogen degradation and many other downstream cellular pathways. Bidirectional motion requires opposing force from the kinesin and dynein motors, causing intermittent Tug-of-Wars (ToWs) followed by runs where winning motors drive their cargo until the next ToW. Dynein displays a counter-intuitive behaviour of catch bonding tightly to the microtubule against opposing force, but why such a response is needed remains unknown. Here we force dynein to catch-bond using an optical trap when dynein-teams are transporting phagosomes in-vitro and inside cells. An unexpected form of collective inactivity emerges, where larger dynein-teams remain inactive for longer after they have been catch-bonded. Kinesin exhibits a high probability of reversing the cargo during such periods of inactivity of dyneins. Therefore, the inactivity of dyneins allows cells to auto-regulate the effect of opposing molecular forces for the purpose of achieving bidirectional motion of endosomes/phagosomes. We propose that an inactivating conformational change is induced when dynein detaches against strain from its catch-bonded state. Collective inactivity follows because each inactive dynein exerts an entropic force on the other to delay the entire team from being activated. We capture the dynamics of this process through a statistical model of Entropically Constrained Reactivation, obtaining predictions in excellent agreement with experimental data. The emergent behaviour observed here possibly prevents a runaway dynein situation inside cells, its simple entropic origin suggesting broader relevance to catch-bonded receptor ligand interactions operating under conditions of cellular crowding.

title: Rab35 drives epidermal wound closure by promoting lamellipodial protrusions and membrane vesicle transport
authors: Schneider, M.; Bogdan, S.
abstract: In response to tissue damage, the epidermal barrier must be restored immediately to prevent excessive blood loss and infections. How cells coordinate actin-driven protrusions and membrane transport during reepithelialization is poorly understood. Here, we identified Rab35 as an important driver of epidermal wound closure in Drosophila. Endogenous Rab35 positive vesicles are directed to the wound edge and in protruding lamellipodia. Suppression of Rab35 function results in striking lamellipodia defects and an accumulation of PIP2-positive vesicles. Depletion of Fascin, a known Rab35 effector phenocopies rab35 knockdown. Upstream of Rab35, we identified CG18659 as potential Rab35-GEF protein, which physically interacts and colocalizes with Rab35. Suppression of Rab35 GEF CG18659 or overexpression of Rab35 GAP Whacked results in strong wound healing defects. We propose model in which Rab35 drives epidermal wound closure by promoting Fascin-stabilized actin-driven protrusions and vesicle transport required for cell membrane expansion and local PIP2 delivery at the wound site.

title: Calpain-mediated regulation of WAVE tyrosine dephosphorylation by PTP61F promotes lamellipodia formation
authors: Milani, W.; Husmann, A.; Bogdan, S.
abstract: WAVE is a major driver of lamellipodial protrusions. Previous studies suggested that Abelson (Abl)-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation of WAVE promotes actin polymerization and lamellipodia formation. Here, we provide evidence that Abl tyrosine kinase rather restricts lamellipodial localization of WAVE and inhibits lamellipodial cell spreading. Additionally, overexpression of a cytoplasmic PTP61F phosphatase increases WAVE localization at lamellipodia tips. PTP61F overexpression or pharmacological inhibition of Abl/Src kinases even protects cells from lamellipodia disruption induced by pervanadate, a potent protein tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor. By contrast, overexpression of a phosphatase-deficient PTP61F trapping mutant phenocopies loss of wave function. We identify the tyrosine Y234 as a prominent phosphorylation site in WAVE. Rescue experiments using CRISPR/Cas9-based KO wave mutant cells confirmed an important role of PTP61F-mediated WAVE dephosphorylation in lamellipodia formation. Our data suggest a model in which calpain-mediated proteolytic release of ER-bound PTP61F antagonizes Abl/Src-dependent WAVE phosphorylation and acts as a mechanism promoting re-localization of WAVE to lamellipodial tips.

title: A genetic anemia disentangles the dual effect of chronically reduced thrombopoietin on hematopoietic stem cells and bone marrow niche
authors: Aprile, A.; Malara, A.; Storto, M.; Gulino, A.; Cancila, V.; Morello, G.; Sighinolfi, S.; Raggi, L.; Beretta, S.; Merelli, I.; Marktel, S.; Ponzoni, M.; Tripodo, C.; Balduini, A.; Ferrari, G.
institution: San Raffaele-Telethon Institute for Gene Therapy (SR-Tiget), IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy
abstract: Many studies unraveled the reciprocal regulation between hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) and the bone marrow (BM) niche by using transgenic knock-out or reporter mice, often overlooking the pathophysiological relevance and the existence of compensatory mechanisms. Here, we exploit the th3 murine model of a genetic anemia, beta-thalassemia (BThal), to investigate the dual impact of chronically reduced thrombopoietin (TPO) production on HSC and megakaryocytic BM niche. Decreased systemic TPO downregulates stemness programs in HSC and impairs their commitment towards megakaryocytes (Mk). We uncover dysmegakaryopoiesis in the BM from BThal patients and mice with defective Mk maturation and reduced production of niche factors, altering the HSC-niche crosstalk. Notably, in vivo stimulation of the TPO signaling restores HSC quiescence, Mk maturation and niche support. These findings demonstrate that TPO regulates HSC through both direct and niche-mediated routes, underscoring the value of using a genetic disease model to disentangle general molecular mechanisms.

title: A gut-on-chip model reveals architecture-dependent epithelial responses to microbial challenge
authors: Nandimandalam, M.; Pandey, P.; Mock, M.; Holzberger, M.; Lochner, M.; Buettner, M.; Bleich, A.
abstract: Advanced in vitro models that better recapitulate human intestinal physiology are needed to improve translational relevance and reduce reliance on animal experimentation. Microfluidic gut-on-chip systems provide controlled architectural and mechanical microenvironments that more closely resemble native tissue than conventional static cultures. However, how these features influence epithelial responses to microbial stimuli remains incompletely understood. In this study, we compared conventional two-dimensional (2D) Caco-2 monolayers with a perfused three-dimensional (3D) gut-on-chip model exhibiting crypt-like epithelial organization. Microbial challenge was employed as a biologically relevant perturbation to investigate barrier-associated responses under distinct culture conditions. Following exposure to the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN), epithelial morphology, barrier-associated gene expression, inflammatory signaling, and temporal response patterns were assessed over time. In a complementary approach, susceptibility to bacterial stress was examined using increasing doses of Citrobacter rodentium (C. rodentium). Both culture systems responded dynamically to microbial exposure; however, differences in response patterns were observed between static and perfused cultures. EcN induced transient alterations in epithelial organization followed by recovery-associated responses, while C. rodentium caused dose-dependent structural and transcriptional changes. Notably, epithelial damage became apparent at lower bacterial loads in conventional 2D cultures, whereas the chip-based model maintained tissue integrity under comparable conditions. Together, these findings indicate that epithelial architecture and the surrounding culture environment influence barrier-associated responses to microbial challenge. The study highlights the utility of gut-on-chip systems for investigating host-microbe interactions and provides a framework for functional comparison of advanced intestinal in vitro models.

title: Chronic nanoplastic exposure causes size-dependent cytotoxicity and ANGPTL4 induction in human kidney cells
authors: Gillings, H. L.; Rojas-Canales, D. M.; Wong, S. W.; Burton, T.; Gleadle, J. M.; MacGregor, M.
institution: Flinders Institute for Nanoscale Science and Technology, College of Science and Engineering, Flinders University, Sturt Road, Bedford Park, South Australia, 504
abstract: Nanoplastics (NPs) are widespread environmental contaminants, yet most toxicity studies rely on short-term, single-dose exposures that poorly reflect daily human exposure. The kidney, particularly the proximal tubule, is a likely site of repeated NP exposure given its role in filtration and reabsorption, but chronic exposure effects are largely unexplored. Here, a long-term in vitro model was developed in which human proximal tubule (HK-2) cells were continuously exposed to 20 nm or 100 nm carboxylated polystyrene NPs (100 {micro}g/mL) over 12 days. Continuous 20 nm NP exposure caused progressive loss of viability whereas 100 nm NPs left viable cell numbers largely unaffected. RNA-sequencing showed 20 nm NPs drove extensive, time-dependent transcriptional dysregulation (1,548 differentially expressed genes at day 6, rising to 4,431 at day 9), far exceeding the minimal alterations in gene expression (35 genes) caused by 100 nm NPs. Cell-cycle analysis and pathway enrichment revealed KRAS pathway activation and S-phase arrest in 20 nm-treated cells, with ANGPTL4 the most upregulated gene. Validation with qRT-PCR confirmed increased ANGPTL4, HMOX1 and FN1 expression, genes implicated in renal fibrosis and chronic kidney disease. These findings show that continuous, size-dependent NP exposure elicits progressive cytotoxic and transcriptional responses in kidney proximal tubule cells and indicate ANGPTL4 as a candidate early biomarker of NP-induced renal stress.

title: MacroH2A1 and H3K27me3 target cGAS to facultative heterochromatin to restrain innate immune activation
authors: Thenin-Houssier, S.; Jahan, C.; Xu, W.; Papadopoulos, G.; Bonnet-Madin, L.; Matsumoto, S.; Kujirai, T.; Cuvier, O.; Kurumizaka, H.; Sobhian, B.; Benkirane, M.
institution: Institut de Genetique Humaine, Laboratoire de Virologie Moleculaire CNRS Universite de Montpellier, Montpellier, France
abstract: The DNA sensor cGAS is largely sequestered on chromatin in an inactive form, but how this state is regulated remains unclear. We show that cGAS preferentially binds nucleosomes containing the histone variant macroH2A1 (mH2A1) marked by H3K27me3 and H3K9me3. Cryo-EM reveals that cGAS selectively engages the mH2A1/H2B acidic patch within heterotypic nucleosomes. Depleting mH2A1.1 or blocking H3K27me3 deposition releases cGAS from chromatin and activates the cGAS-STING-IRF3 pathway. Genome-wide profiling reveals two cGAS-bound chromatin compartments: chromosome-arm sites co-occupied by mH2A1.1, methylated CpG islands, and CTCF, where cGAS and mH2A1.1 binding are interdependent; and centromeric regions (14% of peaks), which lack DNA methylation and mH2A1.1 dependence. These findings establish mH2A1 and H3K27me3 as determinants of cGAS chromatin tethering, linking nuclear cGAS regulation to facultative heterochromatin and opening new avenues for modulating cGAS-STING signaling.

title: Inflammation-driven cellular selection impacts X-linked mosaicism in the epidermis
authors: Ellis, S. J.; Angelopoulou, E.; Gandhi, K.; van Wolfswinkel, M.; Schmautz, L.; Oyarzun, I.; Nowosadtko, S.; Fischer, I.; Schwartz, V.; Griss, J. J.
institution: University of Vienna / Max Perutz Labs
abstract: In eutherian females, the choice of which X chromosome gets embryonically inactivated is thought to be random. Somatic tissues are thus assumed to comprise cells with a 50:50 ratio of maternal:paternal X active. However, a phenomenon known as X-skewing has been observed, wherein tissue composition shifts to be dominated by cells expressing one X or the other. On a gross level, such X-skewing is phenotypically silent except in the case where one X-chromosome carries a disease mutation. Here, by leveraging a mouse model of an X-linked disease called Incontinentia Pigmenti, caused by heterozygous mutations in the NF-kB effector, Nemo, we explore how X-linked cellular dynamics shape progenitor biology in the epidermis. Lineage tracing with X-linked reporters shows that at birth, the epidermis is unexpectedly skewed toward mutant cells. Within a week, as inflammation emerges, these dynamics reverse leaving surviving animals with almost entirely wild-type epithelium. The shift is driven by loss rather than growth since mutant cells adopt an aberrant fate and die at higher rates than their wild-type neighbours; proliferation rises in both populations. Notably, wild-type proliferation scales with local tissue composition, suggesting these cells calibrate their response to the extent of the mutant burden to compensate appropriately for tissue loss. Depleting macrophages, the principal TNF- source, attenuates inflammation, mutant cell death and ultimately is expected to preserve the mutant population. Altogether, our results identify inflammation as a selective force capable of resolving deleterious mosaicism, not only in the context of an X-linked disease, but within any dynamic, clonally heterogeneous epithelium.

title: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition rescues heart function in the Tg2576 Alzheimer's mouse model by ameliorating cardiac amyloid-β pathology and neurotrophic signaling impairment.
authors: Elia, A.; Vazquez-Torres, R.; Carey, A.; Wolf, M.; Gade, V. R.; Alves, M.; Fossati, S.
institution: Temple University Lewis Katz School of Medicine
abstract: FDA-approved carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs) have shown robust efficacy in reducing amyloid- beta pathology, neurodegeneration, and cerebrovascular dysfunction in Alzheimer disease (AD) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) models, highlighting carbonic anhydrases (CAs) as a promising, previously untapped therapeutic target for AD and the vascular contribution to dementia. We have recently shown that amyloid- beta aggregates disrupt neuro-signaling and deplete neurotrophic factors (particularly BDNF) in the heart of AD mouse models and human subjects. In this study, we present the first in-depth examination of CAI therapy (acetazolamide, ATZ) in Tg2576 mice, a well-established model of AD and CAA. We confirm that progressive cardiac fibrosis and amyloid- beta deposition in 13-month-old mice severely impair the cardiac neuro-signaling system, marked by a drastic decrease in BDNF and reductions in adrenergic fibers and regenerating nerve endings (TH and GAP-43 markers), leading to significant declines in ejection fraction and fractional shortening compared to age-matched WT littermates. Critically, this study demonstrates that long-term ATZ treatment in Tg2576 mice significantly reduces cardiac amyloid- beta burden, prevents adverse neuro-signaling remodeling, and restores heart physiological function, as assessed via speckle tracking strain echocardiography. These in vivo findings were corroborated in human cardiomyocytes, in which CA inhibition reduced human amyloid- beta40 oligomer-dependent disruption of CREB signaling, thus preserving BDNF expression. Together, these results reveal a previously unrecognized cardio-neuroprotective role for CAIs in preventing amyloid- beta-induced cardiovascular remodeling and neuro-signaling disruption in the Tg2576-AD model. Given the established benefits of CAIs on cerebrovascular function and cognition, our findings further support advancing repurposing efforts into clinical trials. CAIs such as ATZ could offer a dual-action therapy approach, addressing both the central nervous system and cardiac pathologies associated with AD and, potentially, the systemic effects of amyloidosis.

title: Mitochondrial and metabolic plasticity distinguish stem cells from progenitors in the male germline
authors: Damyanova, K. B.; Fisher, J. J.; Acharya, S.; Nixon, B.; Lord, T.
abstract: Metabolism and mitochondrial remodelling are increasingly recognised as key regulators of stem cell identity, governing the balance between self-renewal and differentiation. Here we compared mitochondrial and metabolic properties of stem and progenitor cells from the male germline using transmission electron microscopy, quantitative proteomics and extracellular flux analysis. While the stem cell-to-progenitor transition was accompanied by increased mitochondrial abundance and cristae density, our analyses unveiled a remarkable and unexpected capacity for spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) to engage oxidative phosphorylation. When oxygen availability was unrestricted, SSCs displayed markedly greater maximal and spare respiratory capacity than progenitors, despite comparable glycolytic flux. SSCs were also enriched for glutathione-dependent antioxidant enzymes and maintained lower basal mitochondrial superoxide levels than progenitors. Collectively, these findings challenge the view that SSCs are predominantly glycolytic and instead identify metabolic plasticity, marked by latent oxidative capacity and enhanced redox control, as a hallmark of the stem cell state.

title: In situ architecture of the basal body reveals regionalized assembly and central pair microtubules nucleation
authors: Wang, Z.; Yang, H.; Lang, H.; Zhu, X.; Zhu, Y.; Sun, F.
abstract: The basal body (BB) is essential for axoneme assembly and ciliary function, and its defects are associated with ciliogenesis disorders and ciliopathies (1,2). However, the molecular basis of the BB's region-specific transitions along the proximal-distal axis, and the mechanism by which ciliary central pair (CP) microtubules are nucleated during ciliogenesis, have remained largely unknown. Here, we resolve the subnanometer architecture of native BBs in mammalian multiciliated cells using cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging, and identify 11 ciliary-base microtubule-associated proteins (CMAPs), including 5 previously uncharacterized core components. These CMAPs localize specifically along ciliary base that facilitate the triplet-to-doublet microtubule transition. We further identify luminal gamma-tubulin ring complexes (gamma-TuRCs) anchored to the microtubule wall via the augmin complex, and propose that they may serve as candidate nucleation sites for CP microtubules biogenesis. Together, these findings define a molecular blueprint of the BB and provide a structural framework for understanding how regional architectural specialization and luminal nucleation collectively drive ciliary assembly and how their dysfunction causes ciliopathies.

title: Spatial organization of fibroblast subpopulations and niches across acute repair and chronic fibrotic remodeling of the human myocardium
authors: Micu, A.; Matei, A.-E.; Li, Y.-N.; Pecher, A.-C.; Filla, T.; Bruch, P.-M.; Dietrich, S.; Henes, J.; Zweck, E.; Eckstein, M.; Klingel, K.; Distler, J. H. W.; Györfi, A.-H.
abstract: Myocardial fibrosis is a common end point of acute and chronic cardiovascular injury, yet the spatially organized fibroblast (Fb) and immune-cell states that sustain fibrotic remodeling across etiologies remain incompletely defined. We applied cyclic in situ hybridization (cISH)-based spatial transcriptomics to myocardial biopsies from patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI), ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), postviral myocardial fibrosis (PVMF), and systemic sclerosis associated primary heart involvement (SSc-pHI). CODEX-based protein imaging provided orthogonal support for cell subpopulations and cellular neighborhoods. Spatially informed clustering identified six Fb subpopulations: COL1A1hi/POSTNhi, NOTCH3+, TIMP1hi, GSNhi/DCNhi, AP1hi Fbs, and myofibroblasts. COL1A1hi/POSTNhi and NOTCH3+ Fbs were enriched in AMI, whereas GSNhi/DCNhi Fbs and myofibroblasts predominated in chronic fibrotic remodeling. These subpopulations displayed distinct extracellular matrix, inflammatory, and vasoregulatory programs. Infarction-associated reparative niches were enriched in COL1A1hi/POSTNhi or NOTCH3+ Fbs and SPP1+ or APOE+ macrophages (M{Phi}), whereas chronic fibroinflammatory niches were enriched in GSNhi/DCNhi or AP1hi Fbs or myofibroblasts with C1Q+ M{Phi} and plasma cells. The GSNhi/DCNhi Fb niche marked areas of subendocardial fibrosis, whereas the AP1hi Fb niche localized to perivascular fibrosis. In SSc-pHI, the actively fibrogenic COL1A1hi/POSTNhi Fb state characteristic of infarct scar formation was present at higher frequency than in other chronic entities and was individually associated with cardiac dysfunction, whereas the chronic GSNhi/DCNhi Fb niche was associated with the extent of interstitial fibrosis and anti-topoisomerase I autoantibodies. These data show that human myocardial fibrosis is organized into spatially distinct Fb subpopulations that assemble into context-specific fibroinflammatory niches across chronic fibrotic remodeling and repair after AMI.

title: A reversible temperature block captures pre-lysosomal intermediates of starvation-induced ERphagy
authors: Molinari, M.; Fabbro, M.; Solda, T.; Morone, D.; Galli, C.; Raimondi, A.
abstract: The selective lysosomal turnover of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) portions, termed ERphagy, removes aged, excess or damaged ER domains. The intermediates forming between receptor activation and lysosomal delivery are short-lived and remain poorly resolved. Here we identify a reversible temperature block at 25{degree sign}C that arrests ERphagy before lysosomal delivery. At this temperature, nutrient restriction still drives focal accumulation of the endogenously Halo-tagged ERphagy receptor TEX264 (puncta formation), segregation of ER cargo, remodelling of the ER membrane, whereas delivery of this material to degradative endolysosomes is strongly reduced. Rewarming above 27{degrees} restores lysosomal delivery, showing that the accumulated eTEX264-Halo puncta correspond to pre-lysosomal intermediates of the ERphagy program. Their formation requires ULK1/2 activity, the ATG7-dependent conjugation machinery, ATG9A, ATG13 and FIP200, coupling receptor clustering to autophagosome biogenesis. Consistently, expansion microscopy and electron tomography reveal curved, cradle-like TEX264-positive ER domains containing ER cargo, co-localizing with autophagy markers and lying adjacent to p62-cargo condensates.

title: Linking live-cell imaging to single-cell sequencing using genetic barcoding
authors: Muller, M.; Lochs, S. J. A.; Apperloo, L.; Banerjee, R.; Fernandes Marques, J. R.; Davo-Martinez, C.; Rullens, P. M. J.; Moreno-Gonzalez, M.; Papageorgiou, V.; Kramer, B. A.; Kops, G. J.; Kind, J.; Tanenbaum, M. E.
institution: Hubrecht Institute KNAW, Oncode Institute, and University Medical Center Utrecht. 3584 CX Utrecht, The Netherlands
abstract: Linking cellular phenotype to genotype and gene expression is a central goal in biomedical research. Live-cell imaging captures dynamic cellular phenotypes, whereas single-cell sequencing measures genome-wide molecular states, but pairing these readouts for the same cell remains challenging. Here we present Waldo, a genetically encoded single-cell barcoding strategy that can be read out by both live-cell imaging and single-cell sequencing to connect single cells across both modalities. Waldo barcodes are generated by combinatorial expression of synthetic cell-surface receptors, each detected by a cognate peptide probe coupled either to a fluorescent dye or a DNA barcode. Iterative fluorescent probe staining achieves large barcode diversity, while preserving fluorescence channels for phenotypic reporters. As a proof-of-principle, we use Waldo to link cell division phenotypes after chromosome missegregation to the karyotype and transcriptome of the same cells. Waldo provides a general strategy for connecting imaging phenotypes to genome-wide sequencing readouts in single cells.

title: Sarcoplasmic reticulum remodeling through autophagosome biogenesis during Drosophila metamorphosis
authors: Kasai, Y.; Borthakur, S.; Bennani, S.; Sakamaki, Y.; Murakawa, T.; Fujita, N.
abstract: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is an elaborate membrane network and the primary intracellular Ca2+ store for muscle contraction. SR abundance, morphology, and spatial organization must be remodeled during muscle atrophy and hypertrophy, yet the mechanisms underlying this remodeling remain poorly understood. Autophagy has been implicated in SR homeostasis and may contribute to this process. We previously showed that a subset of Drosophila larval muscles remodels into adult dorsal internal oblique muscles through an autophagy-dependent process accompanied by extensive SR reorganization. Here, we show that autophagy is essential for maintaining SR abundance and architecture during muscle remodeling. Blocking autophagosome formation caused the accumulation of large aggregates of SR membranes, whereas blocking autophagosome-lysosome fusion led to the accumulation of autophagosomes with SR transmembrane proteins localized to their membranes. Moreover, disrupting LC3-interacting region (LIR)-dependent cargo recognition did not impair SR remodeling, arguing against a major contribution from selective autophagic degradation of the SR. Instead, our findings suggest that SR membrane components are incorporated into autophagosomal membranes during muscle remodeling. We propose that this membrane flow couples the removal of excess SR membrane to autophagosome biogenesis during atrophy, thereby facilitating large-scale SR reorganization during muscle remodeling.

title: iPSC-Derived Myotubes from ME/CFS Patients Reveal Signature Genes, Isoforms and Pathways with Drug Repurposing Potential
authors: Nguyen, D.; Truong, T. T. T.; Panizzutti, B.; Ellis, M.; Spolding, B.; Swinton, C.; Bortolasci, C. C.; Bryce, J.; Smith, J.; Field, C.; Liu, Z. S.-J.; Kim, J. H.; Berk, M.; Walder, K.
abstract: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a complex multisystem disorder. Its hallmark feature, post-exertional malaise (PEM), is a delayed and prolonged worsening of symptoms following even minor exertion. As PEM commonly includes muscle pain, weakness, exercise intolerance and impaired recovery, skeletal muscle dysfunction may contribute to its pathophysiology, but the underlying molecular processes remain poorly understood. We generated induced pluripotent stem cell-derived skeletal muscle myotubes from individuals with ME/CFS (n = 6) and healthy controls (n = 7) to investigate disease-associated transcriptomic alterations and identify potential therapeutic candidates. Myogenic progenitor cells from both groups differentiated into elongated, multinucleated myotubes expressing titin and myosin heavy chain, while qPCR profiling of myogenic differentiation markers further supported successful differentiation. Gene-level analysis identified three differentially expressed genes at an FDR-adjusted p < 0.05: ERVH48-1, CDX4 and SLC2A14. Isoform-switching analysis identified 16 genes with significant differential isoform usage, including CACNA1H, MIEF2, SMAD2 and CHD4. Gene set enrichment analysis identified broader pathway-level alterations involving RNA processing, protein synthesis, proteostasis, mitochondrial quality control, metabolism and muscle-related processes. Library of Integrated Network-based Cellular Signatures Phase 2 (LINCS2) analysis further prioritised 14 compounds associated with mitochondrial metabolism, glucose and lipid regulation, PPAR signalling, calcium and excitatory signalling, neuroimmune activity and cellular stress responses. Overall, ME/CFS iPSC-derived myotubes showed modest gene-level differences alongside broader isoform- and pathway-level alterations, supporting their use for investigating skeletal muscle biology and prioritising candidates for functional validation.

title: Reversible, Orally Bioavailable Small-Molecule Inhibitors Occupy the Substrate Tunnel of the Thioesterase Domain of Fatty Acid Synthase
authors: Fromm, J.; Aleshin, A.; Lambert, L. J.; De Backer, L.; Reddy Ganji, S.; Mattmann, M. E.; Limpert, A. S.; Gosalia, P.; Wimer, C. D.; Layng, F. I. A. L.; Celeridad, M.; Ardecky, R.; Teriete, P.; Scott, D. A.; Hedrick, M. P.; Smith, J. W.; Sheffler, D. J.; Cosford, N. D. P.
institution: Center for Therapeutics Discovery, Cancer Metabolism and Microenvironment Program, NCI-Designated Cancer Center, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Instit
abstract: Fatty acid synthase (FASN) is the sole enzyme capable of lipogenesis in cells and is upregulated in many cancers. Herein we report the discovery and development of SBP-5917 (78S), a novel, reversible, small-molecule probe which targets the thioesterase (TE) domain of FASN. SBP-5917 and other compounds in the series possess IC50 < 1 M and < 5 M for inhibiting recombinantly purified FASN-TE and cellular FASN respectively. Co-crystal structures of our inhibitors bound to the FASN-TE domain show that they are positioned in the substrate tunnel of the enzyme. Biochemical and biophysical analyses quantify the strength of compound binding and demonstrate their selectivity for FASN-TE. Preliminary pharmacokinetic studies indicate promising in vivo potency for many of the compounds in the series. SBP-5917 is the first structurally validated, reversible inhibitor of FASN-TE with demonstrated cellular target engagement and can serve as a chemical probe to investigate FASN as a therapeutic target.

title: Vac8-driven vacuolar remodeling primes mega-autophagy and safeguardsgamete developmental competence
authors: Xiao, T.; Styler, B. S.; Ünal, E.
abstract: During gametogenesis, organelle remodeling is coordinated alongside chromosome segregation to ensure gamete quality. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the precursor-cell vacuole permeabilizes following completion of meiotic divisions, releasing hydrolytic enzymes that degrade cellular material excluded from gametes. The regulation and biological significance of this developmentally-programmed process, termed mega-autophagy, remain poorly understood. Here we identify the conserved armadillo repeat-containing protein Vac8 as a key regulator of mega-autophagy. The presence of Vac8 during meiosis is required for timely execution of mega-autophagy. Specifically, during anaphase II, precursor-cell vacuoles undergo Vac8-dependent fusion to form fewer, larger structures. Deleting VAC8 disrupts this remodeling and impairs subsequent vacuolar permeabilization, establishing meiotic vacuolar fusion as a prerequisite for mega-autophagy. Defective mega-autophagy compromises the ability of gametes to exit dormancy and proliferate upon nutrient repletion. Together, these findings reveal that Vac8-mediated vacuolar remodeling during meiosis primes a post-meiotic quality-control mechanism that safeguards gamete developmental competence.

title: Molecular Force Gates Regulate Mechanical Transmission Across the Nuclear Envelope
authors: Domkam, N.; Yerima, G.; Tsukamoto, S.; Mofrad, M.
abstract: The LINC (linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton) complex is a central mechanotransductive apparatus that physically couples cytoskeletal forces to the nuclear interior, thereby regulating nuclear architecture, chromatin organization, and downstream signaling. Using atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, we identify and characterize force gates within the LINC complex, structural interactions that maintain mechanical connectivity under load. By introducing targeted mutations into the KASH peptide and SUN protein, we provide computational evidence that a key disulfide bond (SUN2 Cys563 to KASH2 Cys6862) and specific residues within the KASH {beta} strand interaction motif (KASH6875, KASH6877) act as distinct mechanical elements during force transmission across the SUN and KASH interface. Leveraging this framework, we show that the disulfide bond and the {beta} sheet network contribute unequally: removing the disulfide reduces both sustained and peak force transmission approximately twofold, whereas disrupting the {beta} sheet network leaves peak force largely intact while altering interfacial coupling and the duration over which load is borne. Localized molecular changes therefore reshape mechanical coupling to the nucleus through distinct routes rather than through a single graded loss of force. Such altered LINC mechanics may be relevant to laminopathies, including Hutchinson Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS), in which defective nuclear lamina compromises force transmission; however, implications for specific diseases remain speculative and require experimental validation. By resolving how distinct molecular contacts contribute to force transmission in space and sequence, this work establishes a framework for dissecting mechanical coupling at protein interfaces under load. These findings provide a foundation for future studies aimed at experimentally testing how individual interface interactions govern nuclear force transmission, a prerequisite for therapeutically targeting LINC mechanics. More broadly, the force gate framework may guide strategies to modulate interfaces that bear mechanical loads in other mechanically regulated proteins. Together, these findings establish a computational framework for investigating force transmission at mechanically loaded protein interfaces and provide experimentally testable predictions for future studies.

title: SNX2, but not SNX1, regulates the hepatocyte growth factor receptor MET in HCT116 colorectal cancer cells
authors: Garcia-Delgado, L.; Derome, A.; Lavoie, C.; Saucier, C.; Denault, J.-B.
abstract: Aberrant signaling of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), including the hepatocyte growth factor receptor MET, contributes to colorectal cancer (CRC) progression and is tightly regulated by endocytic trafficking. We previously showed that combined deletion of the endosomal sorting proteins SNX1 and SNX2 disrupts MET trafficking and enhances downstream signaling in HCT116 CRC cells. However, their individual contributions remained unresolved. Using CRISPR/Cas9-engineered SNX1- and SNX2-KO HCT116 cells, we examined their roles in MET trafficking and signaling. Loss of SNX2, but not SNX1, markedly reduced SNX5 and SNX6 protein levels without affecting transcript abundance. SNX2 deficiency also increased total MET under serum-containing conditions without altering MET transcript or cell-surface receptor levels. Following HGF stimulation, loss of SNX2, but not SNX1, transiently delayed MET trafficking to EEA1+ early and RAB7+ late endosomes, while recycling and lysosomal trafficking remained largely unaffected. This was accompanied by enhanced and sustained HGF-induced AKT activation. Together, these findings identify SNX2 as a predominant regulator of early MET endosomal trafficking in HCT116 cells and reveal functional asymmetry between SNX1 and SNX2. They support a role for SNX2 in spatial regulation of MET signaling through receptor trafficking, consistent with the association of low SNX2 expression with poorer survival in CRC patients.

title: CYB-4/CDK-1 coordinates timing of meiotic entry, chromosome morphogenesis and oocyte maturation in C. elegans
authors: Pezeshki, A.; Jones, S.; Zetka, M.
abstract: Meiotic chromosome segregation requires the earlier coordination of chromosome morphogenesis with cell-cycle progression. In C. elegans, the remodeling of chromosomes in preparation for the meiotic divisions and oocyte maturation is regulated by the master cell-cycle regulator cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK-1). Here, we identify CYB-4 as a meiosis-specific B-type cyclin that is required for CDK-1-dependent functions in meiotic prophase. In a genetic suppressor analysis of a mutant defective in chromosome axis assembly, we isolated a null allele that revealed a function for CYB-4 in regulating chromosome structure at two key prophase transitions. Loss of CYB-4 first delays meiotic entry and the onset of chromosome axis formation, and at pachytene exit delays chromatin condensation, bivalent remodeling, and oocyte maturation. The defects in timely CO formation and bivalent packaging that accompany these delays are ultimately resolved before prophase exit, indicating that CYB-4 is required for the scheduling of events rather than if they occur. Together, our findings provide evidence that CDK-1 activity during meiotic prophase is defined by CYB-4 and support a model in which CYB-4/CDK-1 are essential for the sharp transitions at prophase entry and pachytene exit that coordinate chromosome morphogenesis with meiotic progression.

title: Contact of mobile cis-Golgi network with ER exit sites executes COPI-mediated receptor recycling
authors: Rodriguez-Prieto, R.; Suda, Y.; Tojima, T.; Sabido-Bozo, S.; Kurokawa, K.; Nakano, A.; Muniz, M.
abstract: COPI-mediated retrograde transport is essential for maintaining homeostasis between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and the Golgi in eukaryotic cells. However, its spatiotemporal dynamics remain unclear. In budding yeast, ER export occurs through a hug-and-kiss mechanism, wherein mobile cis-Golgi network (CGN) elements transiently approach ER exit sites (ERES) to capture cargo before departing to deliver it to the Golgi. Here, using high-resolution 3D and 4D live imaging, we show that the COPI-mediated recycling of a cargo receptor from the CGN back to the ER occurs during the hug-and-kiss event. Furthermore, this recycling is complete before the CGN detaches from the ERES, suggesting that COPI-mediated retrograde transport is spatiotemporally coupled to ER export during a single and transient CGN-ERES association. Consistent with this model, when COPI function is impaired, the receptor fails to return efficiently to the ER and instead remains in the CGN after separation from the ERES. Additionally, COPI impairment prolonged CGN-ERES association, suggesting that COPI function also facilitates CGN detachment from ERES. Thus, we propose that rapid COPI-mediated recycling drives CGN maturation directly at the ERES interface, enabling the CGN to detach and proceed along the secretory pathway.

title: One-carbon metabolism sustains effector T cell function through cell-surface glycosylation
authors: Wang, P.; Yu, A.; Mutaher, M.; Eisele, A. S.; Mouche, S.; Hung, K.; Larson, R.; Gish, M.; Zimmer, M.; Brook, J. R.; McNerney, M.; Hammer, L.; Garg, A.; Ozeri, E.; Wong, A. Y.; Petrova, B.; Weitman, M.; Sun, R. C.; Schwartz, M.; Tamburini, J.; Wenes, M.; Hacohen, N.; Kanarek, N.
institution: Department of Pathology, Boston Children's Hospital, Boston, MA, USA
abstract: Folate is a driver of one-carbon metabolism that is essential in T cells. The cellular consequences of its deprivation in CD8+ T cells and impact on anti-tumor function are unknown. Single cell RNA-seq analysis of primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) patients' tumor samples revealed exhaustion in T cells with high folate metabolism gene expression signature. Functional genomics, metabolite profiling, and glycomics identified disrupted cell surface glycosylation as a major consequence of folate deprivation in CD8+ T cells. Mechanistically, folate deprivation reduced nucleotide sugar levels, perturbed glycosylation, and triggered the apoptotic unfolded protein response. Overexpressing folate transporters in adoptively transferred CD8+ T cells increased intratumoral T cell numbers and reduced exhaustion. Therefore, our data draw a mechanistic line between one-carbon metabolism, cell-surface glycosylation, and anti-tumor T cell function, and support a hypothesis that increased folate uptake can enhance CD8+ T cell function including ex vivo and in vivo CAR-T cells.

title: Lactate Promotes Tunneling Nanotube Formation and Reduces Temozolomide Sensitivity in Glioblastoma Cells
authors: Pattnaik, S.; Anand, S.; P, G.; Bera, A. K.
abstract: Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) mediate intercellular communication and contribute to cancer progression. Tumour cells produce excess lactate through increased glycolysis, but whether lactate regulates TNT formation has not been studied. Here, we show that lactate promotes TNT formation in U-87 MG glioblastoma (GBM) cells under both glucose-restricted and glucose-replete conditions, with a similar effect in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells. This effect depends on lactate uptake and metabolism rather than receptor-mediated signalling: inhibition of monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) or lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) reduced TNT formation, while exogenous lactate restored TNT formation during LDH inhibition. 3-chloro-5-hydroxybenzoic acid, an agonist of the plasma membrane-localized lactate receptor (GPR81/HCAR1), did not reproduce the effect of lactate. Lactate also increased intercellular mitochondrial transfer, attenuated temozolomide (TMZ)-induced growth suppression of GBM spheroids, and increased expression of the TNT-associated genes CDC42, MYO10 and FSCN1. Inhibition of p300/CBP-mediated lactylation with A-485 reduced both protein lactylation and TNT formation, implicating lactylation in TNT biogenesis. Lactate increased basal and ATP-linked respiration that persisted during MCT1 inhibition and reduced on LDH inhibition, indicating that the effects of lactate on respiration and on TNT formation are at least partly separable. Together, these findings identify lactate as a regulator of TNT formation and link tumour metabolism to intercellular connectivity and TMZ response, highlighting lactate metabolism and lactylation as potential therapeutic targets.

title: Migrasomes May Originate from Cilia and Represent an Alternative Ciliary Form
authors: zhang, s.; Kutibiding, A.; Wang, M.; yang, y.
institution: The First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University
abstract: Abstract Background Migrasomes, the newly discovered vesicular organelles, have long been speculated to originate from membrane dynamics during cell migration. Here we present integrated imaging and multi-omics evidence supporting a ciliary origin of migrasomes. The shared vesicular trafficking pathways between ciliogenesis and migrasome biogenesis (trans-Golgi/endosomal systems) prompted us to investigate their spatiotemporal coupling mechanism in disease models. Methods Using high-resolution SEM and fluorescence confocal microscopy (FCM), we visualized cilium-like structures with enlarged tips adjacent to migrasome-like vesicles across multiple cell types. TMT-based quantitative proteomics was used to identify proteins shared among migrasomes from different cell types and examine their associations with ciliary proteins. DMBA-induced breast cancer and femoral fracture models were used to investigate the cilia-migrasome association during tumor metastasis and fracture healing. Results Bioinformatics analysis showed a highly positive incidence correlation between cilia and migrasome genes in 31 types of 7858 human normal tissues and organs and various cell types. In 32 cancer tissues, cilia and migrasome genes were still strongly but abnormally correlated. Signaling enrichment by ARL13B and TSPAN4 showed that cilia-migrasome association is related to epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). By analyzing the ARL13B and PIGK expression, we found the abnormal cilia-migrasome association in metastatic breast cancer and positive cilia-migrasome association in fracture healing bone. Conclusion Our findings support a ciliary origin of migrasomes, pointing to a previously unrecognized pathway of organelle biogenesis. Notably, the ciliary-migrasomal association correlates with two distinct pathological/physiological contexts: (1) aberrant epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in metastatic breast cancer, and (2) accelerated regeneration during fracture healing and tissue repair. This dual correlation not only establishes a mechanistic link between ciliary function and migrasome biogenesis but also highlights their divergent roles in disease progression versus tissue homeostasis. Investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of this association may provide novel therapeutic targets for metastatic malignancies and regenerative medicine.

title: Prenatal Alcohol Exposure Downregulates Focal Adhesion Molecules Tensin 1 and Tensin 2 Contributing to Cerebrovascular Dysfunction
authors: Justice, R. J.; Gardiner, A. S.
abstract: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD) are caused by prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE), which leads to developmental defects during embryogenesis. Angiogenesis is one facet of development that is heavily dysregulated during PAE and where such impairment is poorly understood. Here we found that expression levels of focal adhesion molecules Tensin 1 (Tns1) and Tensin 2 (Tns2) were significantly reduced by alcohol exposure in brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMVECs). We also found that miR-150-5p, which we previously found was increased by PAE, regulates the expression of Tns1 and Tns2. Dual-luciferase assays demonstrated direct binding of miR-150-5p to the 3UTRs of Tns1 and Tns2. Additionally, we utilized sprouting angiogenesis bead assays to evaluate endothelial cell sprouting in response to ethanol (EtOH) treatment and following Tns1 and/or Tns2 overexpression as well as miR-150-5p modulation. Tns1 and Tns2 rescued both EtOH- and miR-150-5p-mediated deficits in sprouting angiogenesis. Overall, we found that miR-150-5p negatively regulates Tns1 and Tns2 in BMVECs and that augmenting Tns1 and Tns2 expression may reverse the negative effects of EtOH, and subsequent miR-150-5p elevation, thus improving endothelial cell sprouting during cerebrovascular development.

title: DNA replication stress redistributes the histone methyltransferase G9a and activates lineage-specific gene expression
authors: Oaks, G. E.; Do, B. T.; Jakubicka, E. M.; Cunniff, P. J.; Ward, A. P.; Choplick, C. M.; Nelson, S. A.; Bauer, D. E.; Vander Heiden, M. G.
institution: Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA USA
abstract: Perturbations that cause DNA replication stress can induce lineage-specific changes in gene expression. Specifically, DNA replication stress activates primed loci in euchromatin that are epigenetically silenced, but the mechanism linking stalled replication forks to the activation of distal genes remains unknown. Using reactivation of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) by hydroxyurea in erythroid progenitors as a model, we find that redistribution of the repressive histone methyltransferase G9a from cis-regulatory elements to stalled replication forks increases transcription of the gamma-globin genes HBG1 and HBG2, explaining how hydroxyurea increases HbF expression and benefits patients with sickle cell anemia. In addition to loss of HBG1/2 silencing, redistribution of G9a also increases expression of a primed, GATA1-driven transcriptional program. G9a and H3K9me2 accumulate at stalled replication forks in a manner dependent on the DNA-binding protein WIZ. Overexpression of G9a partially reduces the impact of G9a redistribution on HBG1/2 transcript levels. Together, these findings support a model in which stalled replication forks recruit corepressors away from primed genes, thereby facilitating their activation and explaining how DNA replication stress promotes lineage-specific changes in gene expression.

title: Single-Cell Behavioromics Enables Fate Prediction of Individual Hematopoietic Stem Cells
authors: Chankhunthod, A.; Sorenson-Graff, R.; Mercoli, J.; Ishida, T.; Dozono, S.; Wellington, R.; Fong, Y.; Hadland, B.; Zhao, H. G.
abstract: Achieving near-single-cell precision in the prospective identification of long-term engrafting hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs) remains challenging, likely because current static, point-in-time single-cell phenotyping technologies do not capture the dynamic nature of cell fate decisions. Here, we overcome this barrier by longitudinally tracking individual hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in ex vivo niche cultures using live imaging, coupled with downstream immunophenotyping, single-cell transcriptomics, and transplant assays. Deep learning analysis of live imaging data achieved 98.5% average precision in predicting serially-engrafting LT-HSC (serial-LT-HSC) identity from the behaviorome (the totality of observed behaviors) of each cell, outperforming currently available technologies. Serial-LT-HSCs exhibited lower motility among HSPC populations, which was associated with reduced Activin signaling activity and elevated expression of cell adhesion genes. Correspondingly, antagonizing Activin signaling by Inhibin-A treatment in ex vivo niche cultures suppressed HSPC motility while increasing the frequency of post-expansion serial-LT-HSCs, revealing a novel role for Activin signaling in HSPC behavior and fate determination. Collectively, this study establishes a broadly applicable framework that connects behavioromic analysis and single-cell transcriptomics to enable near-single-cell precision in predicting stem cell fate and uncover molecular mechanisms governing behavior-fate relationships.

title: Phosphoproteomics profiling of the monocytes uncovers the mechanosensory pathways regulating monocytes responses to pathologic level of shear stress
authors: Lai, A. L.; Chheang, C.; Fang, H.; Danish, H.; Mirzaalikhan, Y.; Dayawansa, N.; Watson, A.; Noonan, J.; Ang, C.-S.; Greening, D.; Peter, K.; Baratchi, S.
abstract: Background: Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is the most common valvular heart disease in older adults and currently has no approved pharmacological therapy to prevent or slow disease progression. Aortic valve replacement, either surgically or by transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), therefore remains the only effective treatment for severe CAVD. Monocytes play an important role in driving inflammation and disease progression in CAVD. As the disease progresses and the aortic valve becomes increasingly stenotic, circulating monocytes passing through the narrowed valve are repeatedly exposed to pathological haemodynamic forces, including markedly elevated shear stress, before their recruitment into the valve tissue. However, how exposure to these mechanical forces reprograms circulating monocytes influences their subsequent responses within the valve remain poorly understood. Methods and Results: In this study, we used an engineered model of aortic valve stenosis combined with phosphoproteomic profiling to investigate how prolonged exposure to pathological shear stress reprograms circulating monocytes and influences their subsequent phenotype and function following recruitment into the valve matrix. We further used TAVI as a unique clinical model to determine whether restoration of physiological haemodynamics in patients with severe aortic stenosis reverses the shear-induced monocyte phenotype observed in our experimental model. We found that prolonged exposure of monocytes to pathological shear stress induced extensive remodelling of the proteomic and phosphoproteomic landscape, with enrichment of pathways associated with cellular metabolism, cytoskeletal organisation, and inflammatory signalling. Kinase activity analysis further identified increased protein kinase C (PKC) activity accompanied by suppression of AKT signalling. Consistent with these molecular changes, pathological shear stress increased actin polymerisation, mitochondrial membrane potential, intracellular calcium signalling, and PKC activity. Using a bioengineered extracellular matrix model that recapitulates the glycosaminoglycan-rich microenvironment of the stenotic aortic valve we found that prior exposure to pathological shear stress altered monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation, reducing oxidised LDL uptake and foam-cell formation while promoting co-expression of CD80 and CD163, indicative of a mixed macrophage phenotype. Finally, using a myeloid-specific Piezo1 knockout mouse model, we identified Piezo1 as a key mechanosensor linking pathological shear stress to PKC activation, mitochondrial responses, and persistent changes in monocyte phenotype following migration into the extracellular matrix. Conclusions: These findings establish a mechanistic link between abnormal valve haemodynamics, metabolic and inflammatory reprogramming of circulating monocytes, extracellular matrix remodelling, and immune dysregulation during CAVD progression, highlighting monocyte mechanotransduction and downstream PKC/Piezo1 signalling as potential therapeutic targets.

title: Tracing the dynamic recruitment trajectory of Optineurin between the centrosome and other macromolecular assemblies, signifying its role in cell cycle progression
authors: Chakraborty, A.; Kundu, K.; Weil, D.; Kundu, B.
abstract: Spatiotemporal allocation and dynamic redistribution of centrosomal proteins are critical for coordinating the structural and molecular events that ensure successful cell division. While depletion of the multifunctional protein Optineurin (OPTN) impairs cell-cycle progression, our previous report of the presence of OPTN at key cell-division assemblies raised the question of how its trafficking is coordinated during cell division. In this study, using cell-cycle synchronisation coupled with flow cytometric analysis and confocal microscopy, we report that OPTN progressively dissociates from centrosomes during mitosis, redistributes to cytokinetic structures, accumulates at the spindle midzone, and then concentrates at the midbody during cytokinesis. Moreover, following this transition, OPTN progressively re-emerges at centrosomes during G1 of the subsequent cell cycle. Further, microtubule perturbation and regrowth assays provide evidence that OPTN recruitment and retention at the pericentriolar matrix (PCM) can occur independently of microtubules, whereas its exit is microtubule-dependent. Collectively, this study depicts, for the first time, a detailed movement trail of OPTN, highlighting its centrosome-linked redistribution and microtubule dependency. This context-dependent localisation and trafficking of OPTN across the centrosome-midbody axis establish a definitive spatiotemporal roadmap that can be strategically utilised to study its functional role in cell division.

title: A dsRNA Virus Converts Early Endosomes into Stable Replication Organelles Through Maturation Arrest and Retrograde Transport
authors: Gimenez, M. C.; Ferrero, D.; Issa, M.; Moussaoui, S.; Cabrini, M.; Reboucas Paixao, A.; Liu, L.; Ganesan, S.; Acharya, D.; Boermel, M.; Zaremberg, V.; Verdaguer, N.; Terebiznik, M.
abstract: Infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV) and infectious pancreatic necrosis virus (IPNV) are major animal pathogens that impose a heavy burden on the poultry and aquaculture industries. Yet, major aspects of their unique replication program remain unknown. IBDV is unusual among double-stranded RNA viruses in that it replicates in association with host endosomes. We previously demonstrated this association to be orchestrated by the viral protein VP3 and the early endosomal lipid phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate [PtdIns(3)P], suggesting an essential role for VP3 in forming birnaviruses specialized replication compartments. Here, combining high-resolution fluorescence and correlative light-electron microscopy with diverse molecular and biochemical analyses, we define how the IBDV protein VP3 targets and remodels host endosomes, and establish that endosome-associated replication is conserved in members of the Birnaviridae family. We show that IBDV VP3 targets early endosomes via the PtdIns(3)P effector Early Endosomal Antigen 1 (EEA1) to arrest their maturation and prompt their association with the Golgi complex via ESCPE-1-mediated retrograde transport. We further show that IPNV also exploits endosomal membranes for replication in a PtdIns(3)P dependent manner, although for this virus VP3 engages endosomes through an EEA1-independent mechanism yet to be determined. This work uncovers how birnaviruses exploit a single viral protein to orchestrate endosome remodeling and intracellular trafficking to establish specialized replication compartments while revealing both conserved and host-adapted features of birnaviruses replication.

title: A reversible GNAS-PKA-RUNX2 checkpoint governs skeletal stem cell fate in fibrous dysplasia
authors: Cardenas-Alcoser, E. S.; Rodriguez, D.; Solis, A.; Sato, K.; Ishikawa, T.; Adame-Garcia, S. R.; Ochiai, T.; Koeckenberger, J.; Shin, S. H.; Du, J.; Ferguson, F.; Gutkind, J. S.
institution: Moores Cancer Center, University of California San Diego. Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, University of California San Diego
abstract: Fibrous dysplasia (FD) arises from activating GNAS mutations that increase cAMP signaling in skeletal stem/progenitor cells (SSPCs), but the underlying mechanisms and whether the resulting fate imbalance can be reversed remain unclear. Using controlled GNAS induction with transcriptomic, pharmacologic, and cell-fate analyses, we identify a PKA-dependent checkpoint governing SSPC lineage commitment. GNASR201C redirects SSPCs toward osteoclastogenesis while suppressing osteoblast maturation; genetic or pharmacologic PKA inhibition reverses both effects, revealing this fate decision is dynamically reversible. Mechanistically, PKA phosphorylates RUNX2, the master regulator of osteogenesis, enforcing its cytoplasmic retention and blocking osteogenic transcription; a non-phosphorylatable RUNX2 mutant restores nuclear localization and osteoblast differentiation, defining RUNX2 phosphorylation as a disease-initiating molecular switch. Critically, PKA inhibition in vivo reduces fibrosis and osteoclast burden in established bone lesions, demonstrating reversibility even in advanced FD. These findings define a druggable GNAS-PKA-RUNX2 checkpoint and identify PKA inhibition as a strategy to reverse existing disease in FD.

title: Intrinsic dimensionality of deep learning representations reveals cell death-associated heterogeneity in Parkinsons disease iPSC-derived neurons
authors: Choi, M. L.; Kang, S.; Park, J.
institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
abstract: As AI is increasingly used to stratify heterogeneous Parkinsons disease, it is essential to determine whether learned representations preserve disease-relevant variation within diagnostic or genetic groups. In iPSC-derived neurons from three familial PD cases, deep learning representations encoded an independent measure of cell death, and their intrinsic dimensionality increased with death burden. Latent dimensionality offers a way to examine heterogeneity before AI-derived clusters are interpreted as disease subtypes.

title: A tonic PDGFA-dependent niche organizer maintains alveolar homeostasis
authors: Frabotta, R. S.; Konkimalla, A.; Whitlow, T.; Tsuge, K.; Liu, S.; Forrester, M. T.; Tata, A.; Tata, P. R.
institution: Department of Cell Biology, Duke University School of Medicine, Durham, NC 27710, USA; Duke Regeneration Center, Duke University, Durham, NC 27710, USA; Divisio
abstract: Tissue homeostasis requires mechanisms that preserve quiescence while allowing rapid activation after injury, but how tissues actively restrain injury responses during homeostasis remains poorly understood. Here we identify alveolar type 1 (AT1) cells as organizers of the distal lung niche through tonic expression of PDGFA, which maintains alveolar fibroblast identity and restrains myofibroblast activation. Cell type-specific ablation revealed that loss of AT1s, but not other major alveolar cell populations, was sufficient to evoke spontaneous fibroblast activation and tissue-wide responses that recapitulate injury. In silico ligand-receptor analysis, ex vivo screening, and conditional genetic models identified AT1-derived PDGFA as a key homeostatic signal. Loss of AT1-derived PDGFA caused spontaneous myofibroblast induction and tissue remodeling, whereas increasing PDGFA promoted fibroblast proliferation while suppressing myofibroblast differentiation. Integrated phosphoproteomic, transcriptomic, and chromatin accessibility analyses showed that PDGFA engages SHP2-ERK signaling, suppresses MRTFA-associated SRF programs, and promotes E2F-associated cell-cycle programs, thereby opposing the pro-fibrotic effects of TGF{beta}-driven fibroblast activation. Restoring PDGFA signaling abrogates myofibroblast features from human idiopathic pulmonary fibrotic lungs and attenuated fibrotic remodeling in vivo. These findings define a tonic AT1-derived PDGFA signal that maintains alveolar homeostasis and offers a therapeutic target to prevent or revert lung fibrosis.

title: ESX-1 remodels the Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen storage compartment in macrophages
authors: Luk, C. H.; Auchynnikava, T.; Fearns, A.; Ortiz Canseco, J.; Lockwood, P. K.; Charoy, C.; Gutierrez, M. G.
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) secretes antigenic proteins that drive protective T cell responses, yet how Mtb intracellular localization affects the trafficking and spatiotemporal distribution of mycobacterial antigens in macrophages remains elusive. Here, we developed a split fluorescent protein reporter to monitor the dynamics of the TB vaccine lead antigen Ag85B in infected human macrophages. We discovered that Mtb triggers the formation and remodeling of two distinct types of Mtb Antigen Storage Compartment (MASC) that retains Ag85 within macrophage membranes. Using subcellular spatial proteomics, we profiled the composition of the MASC, identifying both the Mtb and macrophage proteins that constitute these compartments. Unexpectedly, MASCs are defined by metabolic compartmentalization and rewiring to lipid metabolism in both the macrophage and Mtb. Thus, Mtb builds via the ESX-1 system a metabolically distinct antigen storage compartment in immune cells, with potential implications for antigen selection and delivery in TB vaccine development.

title: Patronin condensation integrates recognition, protection and organization of microtubule minus ends
authors: Zhang, B.; Yang, J.; Yu, S.; Zhou, K.; He, L.; Huang, L.; Liang, X.; Wang, H.; Chen, J.
institution: MOE Key Laboratory of Model Animals for Disease Study, Department of Laboratory Medicine, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, The Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Univer
abstract: Microtubule minus ends are central to non-centrosomal microtubule organization, yet how their recognition, protection and molecular organization are integrated remains unclear. Here we show that Drosophila Patronin forms dynamic condensates at microtubule minus ends through a prion-like domain (PrLD). PrLD-mediated condensation cooperates with the CKK domain and a second CKK-independent recognition region to convert weak or broadly distributed microtubule-binding activities into persistent minus-end recognition and tracking. Replacing the PrLD with a heterologous phase-separating HNRNPA1 IDR restores minus-end targeting, indicating that condensation capacity rather than PrLD primary sequence is critical. Patronin condensates further form a protective cap that resists minus-end depolymerization and recruit the cytoskeletal regulators Sas-4, Katanin and Ena. Disrupting PrLD multivalency impairs Patronin localization at multiple developmental sites and causes early organismal lethality. Thus, Patronin condensation creates a physiologically essential microtubule minus-end compartment coupling end recognition, stabilization and cytoskeletal organization.

title: TriPort tangential flow filtration: a lab-assembled system for EV isolation across diverse cell-culture sources
authors: Mainali, D.; Hade, M. D.; Ge, A.; Ezzarouli, H.; Maksour, S.; Thompson, L.; Moreno, C. L.; Neely, G. G.; Hallal, S.; Goldsbury, C.; Magana, S.; Piccio, L.
institution: School of Medical Sciences, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW, Australia
abstract: Tangential flow filtration (TFF) is an effective method for scalable EV isolation. Here, we describe and validate a reference protocol for TriPort-TFF, a laboratory-assembled TFF system featuring a three- port reservoir design enabling sample circulation, retentate return, and diafiltration. Constructed from individually sourced, commercially available components with detailed assembly and operating parameters, TriPort-TFF can be built at a lower cost than commercially integrated TFF platforms. We evaluated the system using conditioned media (CM) from human MDM cultured with EV-depleted human serum, human cerebral organoids in serum-free medium, and mouse BMDM cultured with EV-depleted foetal bovine serum (FBS) unstimulated or LPS-stimulated. The system reproducibly isolated EVs from all three sources, and biological replicates of BMDM showed distinct proteomic clusters between LPS-stimulated and unstimulated conditions. The requirement for subsequent size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) after TFF depended on the sample serum-presence. In serum-containing CM, TFF alone co-concentrated serum proteins alongside EVs, subsequent SEC improved the particle-to- protein ratio, reduced inter-replicate variability and improved proteomic depth. TFF alone in serum- free organoid CM already yielded higher particle-to-protein ratios than TFF-only preparations from serum-containing CM, with SEC further improving this ratio. TriPort-TFF offers an accessible system for EV-isolation that can be combined with SEC for diverse sample types.

title: TMEM209/NPP-28 partitions PLK-1 between the nuclear envelope and nuclear interior during mitosis
authors: Puccini de Castro, V.; Barger, S. R.; Azamfirei, R.; Su, T. Y.; Green, R. A.; Biggs, R. J.; Moore, F. E. Q.; Lee, S.; Oegema, K.; Lara-Gonzalez, P.; Bahmanyar, S.
abstract: The onset of mitosis in animal cells is marked by nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD), which requires coordinated disassembly of nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) and the nuclear lamina. Polo-like kinase 1 (Plk1/PLK-1) initiates NEBD through phosphorylation of NPC components, but mechanisms that spatially regulate PLK-1 between NPCs and the nuclear interior are unclear. Here, we identify the Caenorhabditis elegans TMEM209 homolog NPP-28 as a transmembrane nucleoporin that concentrates PLK-1 at the nuclear envelope while limiting its nuclear accumulation to promote NEBD. We identify docking sites within NPP-28 that mediate PLK-1 nuclear envelope-association. NPP-28 is phosphorylated by PLK-1 in vitro, and mutational analysis suggests that NPP-28-mediated docking facilitates NEBD, whereas phosphorylation prevents premature NEBD. Simultaneous loss of npp-28 and the transmembrane nucleoporin npp-12/gp210 exacerbates mitotic NEBD defects in early embryos and causes severe defects in germline development. Together, our findings identify NPP-28 as a spatial regulator of PLK-1 during mitosis with functional relationships with other conserved transmembrane nucleoporins depending on context.

title: NucLogic: Logic-based geometric 3D nuclear segmentation for fast and robust analysis of challenging biological imaging data
authors: van Dijk, S. G.; Ledesma-Terron, M.; Kraus, S. J.; van Brussel, R.; Marquez Legorreta, E.; Kemp, L. J. S.; Suijkerbuijk, S. J.
abstract: Nuclear segmentation in 3D microscopy remains challenging, particularly for low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) data from timelapse imaging, in vivo experiments, or dense tissue samples. Yet accurate 3D nuclear segmentation is a prerequisite for quantitative single-cell analysis, making this a key bottleneck for high-throughput study of challenging datasets. We present NucLogic, a fast and robust 3D nuclear segmentation algorithm that combines the maturity of 2D segmentation with geometric stitching rules based on nuclear shape, orientation, and intensity, to reconstruct accurate 3D volumes. NucLogic reliably segments challenging datasets including long-term timelapse imaging of organoids, and large dense structures such as the zebrafish brain. Benchmarked against other state-of-the-art segmentation tools, NucLogic matches F1 scores at high SNR, with increasing outperformance as SNR decreases. Importantly, segmentation completes at 20-50% of the computation time, with greater speed gains on larger images. Beyond segmentation, NucLogic includes an intuitive graphical user interface allowing non-experts to segment, quantify, and visualize 3D and 4D data. This enables easy quantification of cell numbers and integration of a variety of both cell-intrinsic properties, such as phenotype, morphology, and local environment metrics, including density and spatial interactions. Together, NucLogic makes quantitative 3D nuclear analysis of previously unmanageable datasets accessible to a broad research community.

title: Recapitulating the notochord to nucleus pulposus transition from human mesendoderm progenitors in 3D
authors: Warin, J.; Vedrenne, N.; Guidoux, B.; Chedeville, C.; Blanche, M.; Maillard, C.; Chariau, C.; Dube, C.; Desprat, R.; Gantenbein, B.; Richardson, S. M.; Guicheux, J.; David, L.; Tryfonidou, M. A.; LEMAITRE, J.-M.; CAMUS, A.
abstract: Intervertebral disc (IVD) degeneration, a major cause of low back pain, is driven by the disruption of nucleus pulposus (NP) tissue homeostasis. The NP arises from embryonic notochord cells that differentiate and adapt to the hypoxic, matrix-rich environment of the developing disc. Recapitulating the developmental trajectory from notochordal progenitors to NP-like cells in vitro remains challenging, as most protocols bypass early specification steps and fail to capture this understudied lineage. Here, using a three-dimensional (3D) system, we reconstruct this developmental path from human pluripotent stem cells into mesendoderm progenitor cells (MEPCs), notochord-like cells (NLCs), and NP-like cells, guided by single-cell transcriptomics and spatial profiling. We identify MEPCs as a distinct progenitor population with a unique gene signature and conserved regulatory networks (GSC, KLF8, LHX1, MIXL1) shared with early organizer and mesendodermal cells. Self-organization in MEPCs-derived aggregates induced spontaneous expression of NOTO, a key transcription factor orchestrating notochordal identity, and enhanced commitment to notochordal fate. Long-term culture in a medium containing TGF-{beta}1 and GDF-5 promoted maturation into SOX9+, KRT8+, CD109+ NP-like cells exhibiting robust matrix deposition and prominent LAMP1-positive intracytoplasmic vacuoles. This scalable, physiologically relevant model enables fundamental studies of human disc biology and early degenerative processes, while advancing regenerative strategies.

title: Peroxisome quality control is gated by a dynamic ATF6α-ABCD3 tether
authors: Noddings, C. M.; Mukherjee, R.; Peukert, C.; Laughlin, T. G.; Wang, J.; Walters, B. T.; Lu, T.-W.; Croll, T.; Eismann, D.; Harel, S.; Xu, A.; Kim, K.; Gupta, M.; Crawford, J.; Arthur, C. P.; Itzhak, D.; Costa-Mattioli, M.; Rudolph, J.; Ashkenazi, A.; Walter, P.
institution: Altos Labs; Buck Institute for Research on Aging (current)
abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) coordinates protein folding and lipid biosynthesis, while peroxisomes govern fatty-acid catabolism and redox balance. However, little is known about the mechanisms by which these organelles communicate. Here we show that activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6), a cytoprotective ER-resident sensor of the unfolded protein response (UPR), forms a molecular tether that zippers the ER and peroxisomes together at a 23-nm intermembrane distance. ATF6 achieves this by inserting a short segment of its unstructured N-terminal cytosolic tail into the solvated transmembrane cavity of the peroxisomal ABC-type lipid transporter ABCD3, trapping it in an off-state. This interaction is reinforced by Ceapin, a previously identified small molecule molecular-glue ligand, which promotes ER-peroxisome contact formation. The junctions serve as a scaffold that can initiate peroxisome turnover by p62-triggered autophagy (pexophagy), as enhanced lipid processing resulting from organelle zippering leads to peroxisome damage due to excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. These findings define ATF6 as a non-transcriptional regulator of organelle quality control and provide a template for engineering Ceapin analogues against ATF6/ABCD3-dependent colorectal and hepatocellular cancers and related diseases.

title: Conserved Fibroblast Subsets Drive Shared Fibrotic Mechanisms in Osteoarthritis Synovium and Systemic Sclerosis Skin
authors: Mohan, A.; Newton, M. D.; Bhate, N.; Khmelevskaya, A.; Hanna, T. M.; DiCarlo, E.; Ospelt, C.; Orange, D.; Varga, J.; Maerz, T.
institution: Institute for Biomechanics, Department of Health Sciences and Technology, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) and systemic sclerosis (SSc) are diseases with distinct etiologies but similar disease phenotypes, most prominently fibrosis, a process governed by the pathological activation of fibroblasts. Mechanisms underpinning fibrosis in these diseases are widely studied, though have yet to be directly compared. We employed single-cell RNA-seq and high-resolution spatial transcriptomics to describe the functional plasticity and the range of fibroblast activation states in both diseases. We identified disease-enriched fibroblast subsets conserved in both diseases, including fibrogenic myofibroblast-like cells, chemokine- and cytokine-expressing inflammatory fibroblasts, and lining-like fibroblasts. These subsets exhibited convergent fibrotic programs also observed in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, as well as overlapping osteochondral transcriptional programs. Xenium 5K spatial transcriptomics revealed that conserved, disease-associated fibroblasts reside in highly similar anatomic niches in OA synovium and SSc skin. These consisted of a fibrotic ECM-rich niche harboring myofibroblast-like cells and an inflammatory niche containing inflammatory fibroblasts adjacent to infiltrating immune cells. Disease-associated transcriptional remodeling converged on shared functional pathways and common putative upstream molecular regulators. These findings identify conserved cellular states, spatial niches, and regulatory programs across OA and SSc, suggesting that fibrotic disease is underpinned by shared pathogenic stromal states and candidate targets for therapeutic strategies are applicable across both diseases.

title: The RNA-binding protein TRIM71 Promotes Supporting Cell Reprogramming and Hair Cell Regeneration by Activating Sall4
authors: Li, L.; Huang, H.; Meng, S.; Liu, X.; Wang, Y.; Qiao, R.; Xuan, Y.-Y.; Hu, Q.; Ma, X.-y.; Ma, H.; Dong, S.; Wang, Y.; Zhang, Y.; Sun, B.; Li, J.; Kolanus, W.; Doetzlhofer, A.; Li, X.-J.
abstract: Hair cell (HC) loss in the auditory organ (cochlea) is irreversible and represents the leading cause of deafness in humans. The absence of HC regeneration is primarily due to the limited plasticity of cochlear supporting cells (SCs). Using a novel doxycycline-inducible TRIM71 transgenic mouse model, this study demonstrates that overexpression of the RNA-binding protein TRIM71 promotes spontaneous cochlear HC regeneration in neonatal mice. Experiments in cochlear organoids indicate that TRIM71 reprograms SCs into progenitor-like cells and that this reprogramming is further enhanced by coactivation of follistatin (FST). FST augments TRIM71-induced increases in chromatin accessibility at progenitor and HC-specific gene loci, facilitating their transcriptional activation in SCs. Notably, FST also enhances TRIM71-induced reactivation of Sall4, which, like Trim71, is highly expressed in early otic progenitors. Using cochlear organoids and explants, we show that the early otic transcription factor SALL4 is required for TRIM71-induced HC formation. By contrast, SALL4 overexpression inhibits HC formation by maintaining reprogrammed SCs in an undifferentiated, proliferative state. These findings establish TRIM71 as an activator of HC regeneration in vivo, provide mechanistic insights into TRIM71's role in SC reprogramming, and identify SALL4 as its essential effector.

title: Metabolic commitment to human motor neurons is characterized by mitochondrial depletion and pyruvate rewiring
authors: Torregrosa-Munumer, R.; Turkia, J.; Spirin, D.; Kvist, J.; Saarimaki-Vire, J.; Povea-Cabello, S.; Ermis, R.; Pennonen, J.; Kuuluvainen, E.; Otonkoski, T.; Hietakangas, V.; McWilliams, T. G.; Fernandez-Vizarra, E.; Katajisto, P.; Tyynismaa, H.
abstract: Mitochondrial remodelling is a key feature of neurogenesis in cortical and hippocampal neuronal lineages, yet the temporal control of organellar homeostasis in developing human motor neurons remains poorly understood. Here, we generated a high-resolution temporal resource integrating proteomics, metabolomics, and mitochondrial characterization across human iPSC-to-motor neuron differentiation. This analysis revealed prolonged mitochondrial depletion during early neurogenesis, characterized by reduced mitochondrial content, mitochondrial fragmentation, and lysosome-dependent turnover. This state persisted throughout the neural progenitor stage and was followed by recovery of mitochondrial content during neuronal maturation. During this transition, pyruvate utilization shifted from pyruvate carboxylation towards pyruvate dehydrogenase-dependent oxidation. Pharmacological manipulation of pyruvate partitioning demonstrated that this metabolic switch is required for human neuronal differentiation. Our findings establish a temporal framework for the metabolic control of human motor neuron differentiation and reveal a progenitor-specific state linking mitochondrial depletion to pyruvate metabolism.

title: WNT/β-catenin increases 3D chromatin mobility and reorganisation during posterior cell state transitions
authors: Wurmser, A. A. M.; Mao, L.; Markevych, N.; Agsu, G. G.; Cao, Y.; Zhang, Z.; Jonaitis, M.; De Winter, N.; Simons, B. D.; Madapura, P. M.; Holcman, D.; Boroviak, T. E.; Klenerman, D.; Samarajiwa, S.; Basu, S.
abstract: Chromatin mobility, the exploration of 3D conformations by the chromatin fibre, is implicated in transcription and DNA repair, and is thought to decrease progressively as cells differentiate. Here, combining live-cell 3D single-nucleosome tracking with genomic approaches, we show that chromatin mobility instead changes in a cell-type-specific manner, increasing as pluripotent cells acquire posterior fates. This is accompanied by 3D genome reorganisation, including loss of Polycomb-associated interactions and emergence of CDX2-associated interactions. Withdrawal of posteriorising WNT/{beta}-catenin signalling rapidly reduces chromatin mobility and partially restores Polycomb-associated chromatin interactions, while Cdx1/2/4-null cells fail to acquire these WNT/{beta}-catenin-dependent changes.
